generated.title: Can a Skyscraper Trigger an Earthquake? Scientists Found Something Strange. #shorts
generated.description:
Could a single skyscraper trigger an earthquake? Scientists in Taiwan found something strange beneath Taipei 101.

Taipei 101 is 508 metres tall and weighs roughly 700,000 tonnes. Researcher Cheng-Horng Lin noticed that small local earthquakes beneath the tower became more frequent during its construction and rose sharply after it was completed. Then two felt earthquakes struck beneath the area: ML 3.8 in October 2004 and ML 3.2 in March 2005, about 10 km deep.

The hypothesis: the tower's enormous weight may have helped trigger slip on a hidden "blind" normal fault, inferred from earthquake data beneath the Taipei basin.

But causation has not been proven. The quakes were about 10 km down, where the building's added stress becomes very small, and other scientists argue the seismic record is too short to show cause and effect. The building did not move tectonic plates. It remains a debated hypothesis, not an established fact.

Sources:
- Lin, C.-H. (2005), "Seismicity increase after the construction of the world's tallest building: An active blind fault beneath the Taipei 101", Geophysical Research Letters 32(22): https://doi.org/10.1029/2005GL024223
- Chen, K.-C., et al. (2010), "A Blind Normal Fault beneath the Taipei Basin in Northern Taiwan", TAO 21(3): https://doi.org/10.3319/TAO.2010.01.25.01(TH)
- Parsons, T. (2021), "The weight of cities: Urbanization effects on Earth's subsurface", AGU Advances (USGS): https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70218755

This video uses AI-generated illustrations of Taipei 101 and schematic underground scenes. They are not photographs, and the underground views are not to scale.
